title: Six Months Back in India, NRI Says 'I Don't Belong Here Anymore'
excerpt: An NRI who moved back from the US at their parents' urging opened up on Reddit about loneliness, fading friendships and a life that no longer fits — and the confession struck a nerve with other returnees.
body:
• An NRI who returned to India after years in the United States wrote that six months in, old friendships feel one-sided, the relationship with their brother feels different — and they no longer feel at home.
  • The move back was driven by worried parents who wanted the NRI closer to home; the returnee says the decision felt right at first and does not blame the parents for the outcome.
  • Respondents included other returnees living the same struggle — one nine months back in India — advising patience, exploring new parts of the country, and joining meet-ups and hobby groups to rebuild a social circle from scratch.
  • For anyone weighing a reverse move: commenters and returnee accounts advise budgeting for an adjustment period well beyond six months, building a local network deliberately rather than assuming old ties will hold, and keeping visa routes back open as a backup plan.

The Post That Hit a Nerve

Six months after trading life in the United States for a return to India, an NRI says the homecoming feels nothing like home. In a post shared on Reddit — later picked up by The Times of India — the anonymous returnee wrote that the decision, made largely because their parents were worried and wanted them closer, has left them feeling adrift.

"6 months back in India and I feel like I don't belong here anymore," the post began. "But now I feel incredibly lonely," the NRI continued, describing old friendships that no longer hold their shape. Old friends are absorbed in their own lives; repeated attempts to reach out and make plans have gone nowhere. "I understand that people are busy and that life changes," the returnee wrote, "but after repeatedly trying, it starts to feel like I'm the only one who cares about maintaining these friendships." Even the relationship with their brother, the NRI said, feels different from what they had expected.

"I had built a routine there, had independence, people around me, and a sense that I was moving forward."

— the NRI, in their Reddit post

The contrast with the life left behind is what stings most. The NRI described the America they left as a place where they had independence, company and momentum — and now wonders whether leaving it was the right call. The one thing they won't do is blame their parents. "But emotionally, this transition has been much harder than I imagined," they wrote.

Context & Background

Reverse migration — NRIs relocating back to India after years abroad — has become a recurring theme in diaspora conversations. Some return drawn by family, children, or a sense of cultural pull; others come back when visa pressures or burnout make staying abroad feel unsustainable. A 26-year-old Indian techie on an H-1B in the US recently told The Daily Jagran he was considering returning to India at lower pay because of loneliness and deteriorating mental health — a decision made from the other side of the same emotional ledger.

But returnees report that the second move can be the harder one. A widely discussed Reddit thread featured a senior executive who returned after more than 15 years abroad and described housing, school admissions and municipal approvals as feeling stacked against newcomers, eroding the ambition he had carried home, according to VisaVerge. Others who chose to come back — like the families interviewed by The Better India — say the return worked when expectations were clear: children, ageing parents and family proximity were the goal, not a replication of the life left behind.

Impact & Analysis

What makes this post land is its specificity. It punctures the assumption that reverse migration is simply a matter of coming home — and names the quiet social cost: friendships that moved on without you, siblings who relate to you differently, and a city that remembers you without making room for you.

Psychologists call this kind of dislocation re-entry shock, and for returning NRIs it carries an extra sting: nobody offers sympathy to someone who has moved "home." The NRI's own frame — guilty about missing the US, guilty about feeling lonely while close to family — is the loop many returnees describe. The Reddit replies suggest the way out is forward, not backward: build a new social circle rather than resurrecting an old one.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, this story is a caution against romanticizing the return. The practical lesson other returnees keep repeating is that the adjustment clock is longer than anyone budgets for — and that a support system has to be built, not inherited. One commenter in the thread advised the NRI to explore different parts of India and meet new people rather than rushing a verdict: "Take it slow. Six months is a very short time to judge yourself." Another returnee, nine months back, said they were still in the middle of the same struggle.

"Take it slow. Six months is a very short time to judge yourself."

— a Reddit commenter, in the same thread

What's Next

The NRI ended the post with an open question to others who had made the same move: how did you build a new social life, and how did you decide whether to stay in India or go abroad again? Suggestions poured in — join meet-ups and hobby groups, consider whether a US return is still possible, or look at other countries if it isn't.

The Times of India noted it had not independently verified the poster's claims. But whether or not this particular story is one person's experience or a representative one, the flood of responses suggests it is at least a shared one — and that the hardest part of returning to India may not be the logistics of the move, but the emotional architecture of belonging.
